assessment.nobel_worthiness: Law and finance opened a research programme that links legal institutions (investor protection, legal origins) to financial development, ownership structure and corporate governance. It spans finance, law and economics and political economy. It is a framework backed by new cross-country data, which fits the combination of data creation and explanatory structure that the committee values. Its influence on empirical work and on policy debates about institutions and finance is very large.
assessment.attribution: The core 'Law and Finance' and 'Legal Determinants of External Finance' papers were written by La Porta, Lopez-de-Silanes, Shleifer and Vishny. A three-name cap forces Vishny out, which is a real attribution cost. Shleifer is the intellectual centre of the broader corporate governance agenda. La Porta and Lopez-de-Silanes carried the cross-country legal-origins data work.
assessment.maturity: The foundational papers date from 1997-2000 and have had more than two decades of replication, extension and critique. Recognition would be well matured.
uncertainties: The legal-origins thesis has been criticised on causal identification and on the persistence of origin effects. Later work qualified some claims.
Excluding Vishny weakens the attribution, and the three-name limit is a binding constraint.
Some of the work is less clean quasi-experimentally than the committee's recent preferences might suggest.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Firm heterogeneity and selection reshaped trade theory after Krugman's 1979 and 1980 papers. They explain why only some firms export, why trade liberalisation reallocates activity across firms, and how the gains from trade work through productivity selection. Melitz (2003) is among the most cited trade papers, and the framework underlies a large empirical literature using firm-level data.
assessment.attribution: Melitz supplied the central dynamic industry model. Helpman added the closely related Helpman-Melitz-Yeaple work on exporting versus FDI and the Helpman-Melitz-Rubinstein gravity extensions. Redding has important quantitative and spatial contributions but is less central to the original framework. Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum are not on this ballot but are relevant antecedents.
assessment.maturity: More than 20 years have passed since the key papers. The framework is standard in graduate training and applied policy analysis.
uncertainties: Credit may be contested by the parallel Bernard-Eaton-Jensen-Kortum 'Plants and Productivity' line of work, which is not on this ballot.
Trade was recognised in 2008 (Krugman), so the committee may prefer other fields this year.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Skill-biased and task-based accounts of technological change, together with the 'China shock' evidence on local labour-market adjustment to import competition, changed how economists and policymakers understand wage inequality, polarisation and the costs of trade adjustment. The work combines new data and credible designs with an explanatory framework, and it has had large societal impact.
assessment.attribution: Autor is the central figure across the task and trade-shock strands. Hanson is the trade-shock co-leader with Autor and Dorn. Katz is the senior figure on the education-technology race and wage structure. Dorn is also strongly credited for the China shock but is omitted by the three-name cap. The task framework also owes credit to Levy and Murnane and to Acemoglu and Restrepo, who are not credited here.
assessment.maturity: The key papers span 1992-2016, with the China-shock work about a decade old. Subsequent studies largely confirm the persistence of adjustment costs, though results are debated.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2023 Goldin prize on labour and with the 2024 Acemoglu prize on technology and institutions may reduce marginal appetite.
The magnitude and generality of the China-shock effects remain debated.
The three-name cap forces a choice between Katz and Dorn, and the attribution is inherently multi-author.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The work links optimal tax theory to the empirics of behavioural responses through the elasticity of taxable income and sufficient-statistics formulas. It connects theory directly to measurable quantities and to administrative tax data. It has shaped tax policy debates on top rates, avoidance and evasion, and it is a clear case of identifiable and policy-relevant scientific contribution.
assessment.attribution: Saez is the most central figure, through his work on bunching, top incomes and optimal taxation. Slemrod is the senior figure on the taxable-income and avoidance literature. Chetty and Stantcheva have strong contributions but are more tied to other agendas, and Stantcheva is early in her career. Feldstein, who initiated the elasticity of taxable income literature, is deceased.
assessment.maturity: The core papers are from the late 1990s to the 2010s, and the framework is well established. Newer contributions are still being absorbed.
uncertainties: Saez also appears on the inequality ballot (B010), so his credit is split across agendas.
The taxable-income elasticity is hard to identify, and estimates vary across settings.
Mirrlees and Vickrey were recognised for the theoretical foundations in 1996, so the empirical contribution must be judged as an independent step.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The New Keynesian framework, built on staggered price setting and interest rate rules, is the workhorse of modern monetary policy analysis and central bank practice. Its foundational ideas have had enormous practical and academic influence. The policy-rule analysis and the microfounded treatment of nominal rigidities are central.
assessment.attribution: Calvo (1983) supplied the pricing mechanism. Taylor (1980 and 1993) contributed staggered contracts and the policy rule. Woodford provided the synthesis in 'Interest and Prices'. Gali, Gertler, Christiano, Eichenbaum and Smets are also essential for the empirical DSGE implementation. Any three-name selection leaves out major contributors, so attribution is hard.
assessment.maturity: The foundations are 30 to 40 years old and fully proven in practice, although the framework has been tested by the 2008 crisis and the post-2021 inflation.
uncertainties: The attribution problem is severe: eight credited names, a three-name cap, and several defensible combinations.
Debate persists over the framework's adequacy after the financial crisis and the recent inflation episode.
Macro has been recognised repeatedly (Lucas, Kydland-Prescott, Sargent-Sims), which may weigh against it.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The work measures intergenerational mobility with population-scale administrative tax records, exposes large geographic variation, and links it to neighbourhood and childhood exposure effects. It builds new data on a big social question and is highly influential on policy debates. It is an exemplar of data discovery with identifiable causal designs, though the explanatory framework is thinner than the data contribution.
assessment.attribution: Chetty is the clear driver of the programme. Hendren and Friedman are the main co-authors on the mobility, neighbourhood and exposure-effects papers. Katz is credited here but is more central to B015. Attribution to a large team around Opportunity Insights is complicated, and some credit goes to earlier mobility work by Solon, Corak and others who are not on the ballot.
assessment.maturity: The central papers date from 2014 to 2022. The findings are influential but have had less time for long-run replication, and some neighbourhood-effect claims continue to be tested.
uncertainties: Relatively recent, so its durability is less certain.
Chetty also has contributions in public economics (B003) that could be recognised separately.
Credit division across the Opportunity Insights team and earlier mobility scholars is difficult.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Persson, Tabellini and Besley developed a systematic framework for how electoral rules, constitutions and state capacity shape fiscal policy and public goods provision. It linked political economy theory to cross-country and cross-institutional evidence. It established modern political economics as a core field, and the work has had wide influence on institutional analysis.
assessment.attribution: Persson and Tabellini are the co-authors of the integrating book 'Political Economics' and of the constitutional-rule empirics. Besley is closely associated with state capacity and accountability. The three form a coherent group, though Besley's agenda partially diverges from the other two.
assessment.maturity: The central contributions date from the 1990s to 2000s. The field is mature, with extensive replication and extension.
uncertainties: The 2024 prize on institutions and prosperity (Acemoglu, Johnson, Robinson) overlaps in theme and may reduce appetite.
Cross-country identification of constitutional effects is contested.
Credit division with other political-economy theorists such as Alesina and Acemoglu is possible.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Resume audit and correspondence studies gave credible causal evidence on discrimination in hiring, such as the Bertrand-Mullainathan names study. They also helped shape a wider methodological tradition in labour economics, law and economics and policy evaluation. They are simple, transparent and influential, and they connect to questions of bias and decision making. The theoretical explanatory framework is lighter than the empirical contribution.
assessment.attribution: Bertrand and Mullainathan share the best-known 'Emily and Greg' paper and have wider joint and separate agendas. Charles is credited here for work with Guryan on prejudice, but earlier audit work (Bendick, Neumark, Heckman-Siegelman) and the Becker framework are antecedents. Mullainathan's broader behavioural and machine learning work also raises questions about which contribution would be cited.
assessment.maturity: The central paper dates from 2004, and more than twenty years of replication and field experiments broadly support the existence of discrimination in callbacks. Mechanisms and welfare implications remain open.
uncertainties: Audit designs have known limitations (unobservable productivity differences, callbacks versus hires).
The Nobel-level contribution may be seen as methodological and empirical rather than as a new conceptual framework.
I work in a neighbouring field (labour economics and the economics of crime), so I flag the possibility of familiarity bias.
